title: Perf run 20261015-0212
heading: A phone’s start page shows its board in half the time, and a game’s review finishes in less than half
meta:
On a phone, the start page now shows its board in about 0.9 s instead of 1.7 s. A finished game’s review now marks every move in 4.6 s instead of 10 s. The phone fix is a bug fix: every phone downloaded the tablet’s picture first and the right picture late. The run also fixed four correctness problems on the server and in the client. No headline measurement got worse. Everything is in PR #147.

Run 2026-10-15, 02:12–05:30 UTC. Main at 9f2d524, branch improve/20261015-0212 (pushed as claude/serene-galileo-jajbb3). Measured in headless Chromium with SwiftShader (WebGL drawn on the CPU) on 4 CPUs. Every comparison is an A/B: the bench runs main and the branch back to back several times, and each back-to-back run is a pair. A change is called only when every pair moves the same way, by more than 5% and by more than the pairs disagree with each other.

items.title: Review PR #147, and decide whether to split it
items.body: The PR holds the run’s changes in four kinds. Each commit’s message gives its evidence; six commits hold two related changes each (listed in the run record), not one. CLAUDE.md asks for one logical change per PR; the run’s instructions asked for one branch and one PR. CI passed on the merge commit 89eb146: client, server tests and all three e2e shards. CI on the last head runs as this is written; see the PR for its result.

items.title: The start page got slower on phones with #138; the branch fixes a bug that cost part of it, and two rows need watching
items.body:
Since the last run, six features landed on main. One of them, #138 (the start page’s picture), made “Start page usable, phone” 9.4% slower, called in every pair (776 → 848 ms), while making the board appear about twice as soon. #138 also had a bug, which this branch fixes: the picture’s preload ran before the page knew it was on a phone, so every phone downloaded the tablet’s 73 KB picture beside the page’s code. That explains part of the extra bytes, but not necessarily the slowdown.

Against main, the fixed branch has the phone’s “usable” time 3.4% sooner (final A/B), 0.2% sooner (6-pair re-check) and 6.5% sooner (after the merge), none called. I did not compare the branch with the code from before #138, so how much of the 9.4% is recovered is not measured. “Start page usable, desktop” leaned slower in two A/Bs (+4.0% and +6.4%, every pair of the second above 1, not called) and faster in two (−1.8% and −2.8%). The preload fix moves an inline script in the page’s head, which runs on desktop too, so the branch does touch that path.

items.title: Flag: a review now holds more memory than the bench measures
items.body: The run’s memory rule flags any peak increase over 5%. The page’s own heap did not grow (a reopened long game: −0.1%). But a review now runs up to three workers instead of one, and the bench does not measure workers. By estimate, each extra worker holds its own JavaScript heap and 3.25 MiB of search tables (ledger M9′), so a review on a 4-core machine may hold about 10 MB more while it runs, and frees it when it ends. Against a page heap of about 14 MB that is well over 5%. It is not measured.
items.recommend: Keep the parallel review, and let the next run measure the workers’ memory (Chrome’s memory tools can) and make the search tables once per worker (M9′), which removes most of the per-position allocation.

scoreboard.intro: The bench’s headline measurements are the moments a player waits for, listed in bench/primary.mjs. This run added one: a finished game’s review, from “Analyse” to every move marked. Against main, the branch is 1.097 times as fast over all fourteen. Two are called better: the phone’s start page showing its board (46% faster) and the review (54% faster). None is called worse, but two lean slower than the run’s 3% limit without being called: “Start page usable, desktop” (see Needs from me) and “Reopening a long game” (+9.5%; measured again below, −12% on the last commit). The page’s heap did not grow (−0.1% on a reopened long game); the review’s workers are not measured (see Needs from me).

items.title: The headline results again, on the merge commit
items.body:
After merging main, I measured the start page and the review again on the merge commit 89eb146, against the new main. The last code commit, 9afbf60, changes only the review’s worker count where there are no workers; the review was measured on it too (below), the start page was not. Both results hold: the phone’s board appears at 923 ms instead of 1.76 s (46% faster), and the review finishes in 4.74 s instead of 10.4 s (56% faster), both called. Both “usable” rows leaned faster (desktop 2.8%, phone 6.5%), not called.

One row was called worse: the desktop’s first visit’s first click, 19 → 512 ms. It is timed once per run and has two modes, about 15 ms or about 500 ms, depending on whether the click lands while the first visit is still preparing its shaders. Pooled over the last two A/Bs, the slow mode came up in 4 of 9 branch runs and 3 of 9 main runs, and the 6-pair re-check before the merge called nothing (it leaned 82% faster). Main’s own later clicks hit the slow mode too (370, 555 and 338 ms). I read it as noise that a 3-pair A/B can call either way; the next run times more first visits.

items.title: Reopening a long game, measured again on the last commit
items.body: In the final A/B the headline row “Reopening a long game (2,000 plies)” leaned 9.5% slower (161 → 178 ms, not called), over the run’s 3% limit, and the re-checks after it did not measure it. Measured again on the last commit, 9afbf60, against main de25815: 12% faster (167 → 157 ms, not called), with its first picture −1.8%, its page freezes −2.7% and its heap +0.2%. The lean did not recur. The same A/B measured the review on this commit: 54% faster, called. Seeding the 2,000-ply game takes 4.3 times as long in the bench’s local server, which now copies records as production does; that is bench setup, not a moment a player waits on.

items.title: The branch against the first recorded run
items.body: The run’s target was 1.2 times the speed of the first recorded run (92ce041). The merge commit 89eb146 is 2.17 times as fast over the eleven headline measurements the old code can also make; it had no computer player and no review. Six are called better, most by far: a move or a picked-up piece now appears in about 0.4–0.5 s instead of over 5 s, mostly from the last run’s change to how pictures reach the GPU. Three are called worse than the first run, all on the start page: usable on desktop (78 → 123 ms) and on the phone (709 → 925 ms), and the first click (8.5 → 22 ms). The start page has grown a lot since then (the computer player, the tutorial, the picture), and this run’s fix recovers only part of that. A reopened long game uses 34% more JavaScript heap than in the first run, as earlier runs already found.

items.title: A phone downloads the start page’s own picture, and shows it in half the time
items.body:
The start page shows a picture of its 3D preview until the preview has loaded. A small script in the page’s head starts that picture downloading early, choosing the phone, tablet or wide picture from the window’s size. The build placed the script before the tag that tells a phone to use its own width, and until that tag is read a phone reports a 980-pixel-wide window. So every phone chose the tablet’s picture (73 KB), and the phone’s own picture started downloading only when the page drew it.

The script now follows that tag (commit 0c7aea0). A unit test fails if it moves back, and the bench now counts the pictures each cold load downloads. On the slowed phone, the board appears at 870 ms instead of 1.70 s, the page downloads 12% less, and “Play a friend” is ready 3.5% sooner (not called). One diagnostic got worse. On the phone without slowing, the first paint comes 76 ms later (146 → 222 ms), because the picture has already arrived and the first frame now includes it. The board on that phone appears 8.5% sooner.

items.title: A finished game’s review searches in several workers at once
items.body:
A review searches each position of the game for a fixed number of positions (120,000), so its marks are the same on any machine. It used to search one position at a time in one worker. Each position is a separate search, so they can run side by side with the same results. The review now uses one worker per spare core, at most three, and hands the positions out from the start of the game (commit b305f6d). The marks were identical in all 16 runs of the A/B, and the page showed no freezes.

A review whose search failed used to show “done” with its counts as if final, so a review that failed at the first move read as a perfect game. Now it says “Analysis stopped” with a Retry button, which continues from the positions already found. The diff review found that a search finishing after the stop could restart the progress bar for good; that is fixed with a test (4b7fb96). The grading found that when the review cannot use workers it runs its searches on the page’s own thread, three at a time instead of one. 9afbf60 fixes this only for a browser with no workers at all (with a test). When a worker’s script fails to load (a stale file after a deploy, say), each of the three still falls back to the page on its own, so the page can be busy three times as long. That case is not fixed; it is first in Next.

items.title: The server’s tests now catch a lost write-back, and one large message can no longer stall every game
items.body:
Each change to a game record is read, changed and written back. In production the store hands out copies, so the write-back is the whole change. The tests used a plain dictionary, which hands out the record itself, so a missing write-back passed every test. The tests and the local server now use a store that copies the way production does (commits fea5a5a and 2e17292). Removing a write-back now fails two tests; on main all 77 pass.

Every message is checked against all 31 message types. A 1 MB message made of 100,000 short keys took 7.4 s to check on this machine, and the server handles all games on one thread. Messages longer than 4,096 characters are now refused before they are read (cfbace2); the longest real message is about 150. A rejoin now sends every field the stored record shares with the protocol, instead of a hand-kept list, and its test reads the field from the rejoin (10ce347).

items.title: A focus bug my own cleanup caused, fixed
items.body: Merging the six offer lines into one table (1d1ca66) made React reuse one element for whichever line shows. With a take-back and a draw offer both standing, a keyboard player who declined the take-back kept focus on the same button, which then declined the draw. The diff review caught it, and keying each line by what it says fixes it (4b7fb96). This fix has no test.

items.title: A rematch keeps its seat when the browser refuses to save it
items.body: When local storage was full or turned off, accepting a rematch opened the new game with no saved seat, and the page showed “Game full” for the game the player had just been placed in. The page now also carries the seat in its navigation (9ba343a).

items.title: Checks that can now fail
items.body:
• The grade thresholds are tested a centipawn either side of each edge. A slope 2% off now fails the test (ede4014).
  • Lint now fails any app canvas that does not draw on demand (beccfdf).
  • The start page’s e2e tests now check that the picture decoded, not only that its box is visible (7cbf25a).
  • The bench has a review section, which fails if two runs give different marks (995fca9, fixed in f3a7997).

removed.intro: Nothing was deleted outright. Against main at de25815, the branch adds 590 lines and removes 215 in 30 files, outside the run’s notes. The app’s code grows by 62 lines (client +30, server +32): the parallel review and its stopped state, the rematch’s seat, the preload fix, the size cap and the copying store. Cleanup removed 29 lines from GameActions (six near-identical blocks into one table) and 21 lines of test stubs that nothing read. Tests grow by about 165 lines, the bench by 123 (the review section, the picture count and the probe), lint by 11 and docs by 13. My shared e2e resign helper and level-list change were dropped in the merge, since #144 had made the same changes.

items.title: Loading the 3D preview only after the picture is on screen
items.body: A reviewer suggested that the preview’s code, loading at the same time, held the picture back. Five pairs showed otherwise: the phone’s board leaned 9.8% faster (not called), the desktop’s leaned 27% slower (not called), and the phone’s live preview was called 11% slower. I reverted it; the patch is in bench/loop/patches/picture-before-preview-SP1.patch. Looking at that phone load step by step is what found the real cause, the wrong picture.

items.title: Catching JSON nested too deeply
items.body: I added a catch for this with the size cap. The diff review pointed out that a message under 4,096 characters can nest at most 2,047 levels, which Python parses without trouble, so the catch could never run. I removed it.

choices.intro:
• The review uses one worker per spare core, at most three. On a 4-core phone that is three workers during a review, using up to about 10 MB more memory while it runs (not measured).
  • The words “Analysis stopped” and “Retry” for a failed review.
  • Messages over 4,096 characters are refused with “Message is too large”.
  • The local server, e2e and the bench now copy records the way production does. Seeding a 2,000-move game in the bench takes longer (bench setup only, not a measured moment).
  • I accepted the later first paint on the unthrottled phone, since the board itself appears sooner.
  • The branch is pushed as claude/serene-galileo-jajbb3, the session’s branch, not improve/20261015-0212.
  • I folded the dependencies reviewer into the “what’s new” reviewer: every dependency is current (three r186, react-three-fiber 9.8.1, Vite 8.3.4).

notConfirmed.intro:
• The review on a real phone. With three workers on a slow phone, a position might hit the 1.5 s time limit before its 120,000 positions, and its marks would then differ from a desktop’s.
  • The workers’ memory during a review. The bench measures the page’s memory, not the workers’.
  • Whether Modal’s own front end accepts frames larger than 4,096 characters at all; the cap holds either way.
  • The full e2e suite on this machine. It ran in CI on the merge commit and passed; here I ran the six specs the changes touch (14 tests, all passing).
  • Caching of the built files on Cloudflare Pages. The sandbox cannot reach pages.dev to read the headers.

merge.intro: Other sessions merged three PRs into main during the run (#141, #144 and #145), and more were open. I merged main into the branch at 89eb146. Six files conflicted. #144 had also made one shared e2e resign helper and made isDifficulty read the list of levels, so I took main’s versions and dropped mine. The rematch keeps its colour in the navigation, using main’s otherSide. Lint, typecheck, 1,373 unit tests and 79 server tests pass on the merge. Main moved again at 05:09 UTC (#146, ec44dfa). The branch is behind it but merges cleanly (checked with git merge-tree); I did not merge it, so that the final measurements stay on the commit they measured. ARCHITECTURE.md now describes the parallel review and its stopped state, the picture’s preload, the copying store and the size cap. CLAUDE.md is unchanged.

next.intro:

  2. Measure a review’s time per position on a phone, to see whether the 1.5 s limit bites (RV18).
  3. Count the shaders linked at the end of a reopened game’s entrance, where #140’s replay may have moved three of them (RP1).
  4. Keep a review’s results when the page is reloaded (RV-K).
  5. Make /assets/* cacheable for a year in _headers, after reading the production headers (P2′).
